claim: Adam13/33 is a cell surface metalloprotease critical for cranial neural crest (CNC) cell migration.
source: Adam13/33 is a cell surface metalloprotease critical for cranial neural crest (CNC) cell migration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about adam13/33.

claim: Adam13 can cleave multiple substrates including itself, fibronectin, ephrinB, cadherin-11, pcdh8 and pcdh8l.
source: It can cleave multiple substrates including itself, fibronectin, ephrinB, cadherin-11, pcdh8 and pcdh8l (this work).
evidence: The abstract lists known substrates of adam13, with pcdh8l being a finding from this work.

claim: Cleavage of cadherin-11 by adam13 produces an extracellular fragment that promotes CNC migration.
source: Cleavage of cadherin-11 produces an extracellular fragment that promotes CNC migration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of adam13.

claim: The adam13 cytoplasmic domain is cleaved by gamma secretase.
source: In addition, the adam13 cytoplasmic domain is cleaved by gamma secretase, translocates into the nucleus and regulates multiple genes.
evidence: The abstract describes this as a known mechanism of adam13 function.

claim: The adam13 cytoplasmic domain translocates into the nucleus and regulates multiple genes.
source: In addition, the adam13 cytoplasmic domain is cleaved by gamma secretase, translocates into the nucleus and regulates multiple genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function.

claim: Adam13 interacts with the arid3a/dril1/Bright transcription factor.
source: Here, we show that adam13 interacts with the arid3a/dril1/Bright transcription factor.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: The interaction between adam13 and arid3a promotes a proteolytic cleavage of arid3a.
source: This interaction promotes a proteolytic cleavage of arid3a and its translocation to the nucleus where it regulates another transcription factor: tfap2α.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Arid3a translocates to the nucleus where it regulates tfap2α.
source: This interaction promotes a proteolytic cleavage of arid3a and its translocation to the nucleus where it regulates another transcription factor: tfap2α.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Tfap2α activates multiple genes including the protocadherin pcdh8l (PCNS).
source: Tfap2α in turn activates multiple genes including the protocadherin pcdh8l (PCNS).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The proteolytic activity of adam13 is critical for the release of arid3a from the plasma membrane.
source: The proteolytic activity of adam13 is critical for the release of arid3a from the plasma membrane while the cytoplasmic domain appears critical for the cleavage of arid3a.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of adam13 is critical for the cleavage of arid3a.
source: The proteolytic activity of adam13 is critical for the release of arid3a from the plasma membrane while the cytoplasmic domain appears critical for the cleavage of arid3a.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Adam13 cleaves pcdh8l generating an extracellular fragment that regulates cell migration.
source: In addition to this transcriptional control of pcdh8l, adam13 cleaves pcdh8l generating an extracellular fragment that also regulates cell migration.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Cranial neural crest (CNC) cells are induced at the border of the neural and non-neural ectoderm by a combination of signals including BMP, Wnt and FGF.
source: Cranial neural crest (CNC) cells are a transient population of natural stem cells that are induced at the border of the neural and non-neural ectoderm by a combination of signals including BMP, Wnt and FGF (Dorsky et al., 1998; Monsoro-Burq et al., 2003; Tribulo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BMP, Wnt and FGF signals mediate the expression of key transcription factors that define placodal and neural crest cells.
source: These signals mediate the expression of key transcription factors that define placodal and neural crest cells (Groves and LaBonne, 2014; Milet and Monsoro-Burq, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tfap2α is one of the earliest and most conserved transcription factors that controls the fate of neural border cells and later neural crest cells.
source: Among those the transcription factor tfap2α is one of the earliest and most conserved factors that controls the fate of neural border cells and later neural crest cells (de Croze et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of tfap2α in all vertebrates tested leads to craniofacial defects.
source: While loss of tfap2α in all vertebrates tested leads to craniofacial defects, mutations in the tfap2α gene in humans are associated with the Branchiooculofacial Syndrome highlighting the importance of this gene for craniofacial development and neural crest cell biology throughout evolution (Hoffman et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2003; Martinelli et al., 2011; Meshcheryakova et al., 2015; Van Otterloo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mutations in the tfap2α gene in humans are associated with the Branchiooculofacial Syndrome.
source: While loss of tfap2α in all vertebrates tested leads to craniofacial defects, mutations in the tfap2α gene in humans are associated with the Branchiooculofacial Syndrome highlighting the importance of this gene for craniofacial development and neural crest cell biology throughout evolution (Hoffman et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2003; Martinelli et al., 2011; Meshcheryakova et al., 2015; Van Otterloo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CNC cells migrate toward the ventral side of the embryo to contribute to most of the craniofacial structures.
source: Once induced, CNC cells migrate toward the ventral side of the embryo to contribute to most of the craniofacial structures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CNC cell behavior.

claim: Cadherin-11 is required at the surface of CNC cells.
source: In particular, while cadherin-11 is required at the surface of CNC, an excess of the protein prevents migration (Borchers et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An excess of cadherin-11 prevents CNC migration.
source: In particular, while cadherin-11 is required at the surface of CNC, an excess of the protein prevents migration (Borchers et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of cadherin-11 binds to the GEF trio and promotes filopodia formation in the migrating CNC.
source: The cytoplasmic domain of cadherin-11 binds to the GEF trio and promotes filopodia formation in the migrating CNC (Kashef et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cadherin-11 localizes to nascent focal adhesion and interacts with the proteoglycan syndecan-4 via its transmembrane domain.
source: In addition, cadherin-11 also localizes to nascent focal adhesion and interacts with the proteoglycan syndecan-4 via its transmembrane domain (Langhe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The extracellular domain of cadherin-11 is cleaved by the metalloprotease adam13 producing an extracellular fragment that promotes cell migration.
source: Lastly, the extracellular domain of cadherin-11 is cleaved by the metalloprotease adam13 producing an extracellular fragment that promotes cell migration (McCusker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The cadherin-11 extracellular fragment can compete with the integral cadherin-11 to decrease contact inhibition of locomotion by a homophilic-dependent binding site.
source: This fragment can compete with the integral cadherin-11 to decrease contact inhibition of locomotion by a homophilic-dependent binding site, but this site is not required for its ability to promote CNC migration (Abbruzzese et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The homophilic-dependent binding site of the cadherin-11 fragment is not required for its ability to promote CNC migration.
source: This fragment can compete with the integral cadherin-11 to decrease contact inhibition of locomotion by a homophilic-dependent binding site, but this site is not required for its ability to promote CNC migration (Abbruzzese et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pcdh8l is essential for CNC migration both in vivo and in vitro.
source: In Xenopus, the protocadherin pcdh8l is essential for CNC migration both in vivo and in vitro suggesting that it affects the basic cell locomotion machinery (Rangarajan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pcdh8 (PAPC) can functionally replace pcdh8l in the neural crest cells.
source: Interestingly, the protocadherin pcdh8 (PAPC), which can functionally replace pcdh8l in the neural crest cells (Schneider et al., 2014) is a substrate for adam13 (Abbruzzese et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pcdh8 (PAPC) is a substrate for adam13.
source: Interestingly, the protocadherin pcdh8 (PAPC), which can functionally replace pcdh8l in the neural crest cells (Schneider et al., 2014) is a substrate for adam13 (Abbruzzese et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cleavage of cadherin-6 by adam10 and adam19 is critical for proper migration of neural crest cells in chick.
source: In chick, cleavage of cadherin-6 by adam10 and adam19 is also critical for proper migration of the neural crest cells (Schiffmacher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Adam13/33 plays critical roles in CNC induction in Xenopus tropicalis by cleaving ephrinB.
source: In addition to its proteolytic cleavage of cadherin-11, adam13/33 has been shown to play critical roles in CNC induction in Xenopus tropicalis by cleaving ephrinB, reducing its inhibitory activity upon the Wnt signaling pathway and allowing for a robust expression of snai2 (Wei et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cleavage of ephrinB by adam13 reduces its inhibitory activity upon the Wnt signaling pathway.
source: In addition to its proteolytic cleavage of cadherin-11, adam13/33 has been shown to play critical roles in CNC induction in Xenopus tropicalis by cleaving ephrinB, reducing its inhibitory activity upon the Wnt signaling pathway and allowing for a robust expression of snai2 (Wei et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Knock down of adam13 in Xenopus laevis has no effect on snai2 expression but affects CNC migration in vivo.
source: In contrast, knock down of adam13 in Xenopus laevis has no effect on snai2 expression but affects CNC migration in vivo (Cousin et al., 2011; Alfandari et al., 2001; Cousin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of adam13 is cleaved by gamma secretase and translocates into the nucleus where it regulates the expression of thousands of genes.
source: We have shown that the cytoplasmic domain of adam13 is cleaved by gamma secretase and translocates into the nucleus where it regulates the expression of thousands of genes.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: The cleavage of adam13 cytoplasmic domain by gamma secretase requires a self-proteolytic cleavage by adam13 in its own cysteine rich domain.
source: The cleavage by gamma secretase requires a self-proteolytic cleavage by adam13 in its own cysteine rich domain and is therefore dependent on the adam13 proteolytic activity.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: In the absence of the cytoplasmic domain, adam13 cannot support CNC migration.
source: In the absence of the cytoplasmic domain, adam13 cannot support CNC migration, but addition of a soluble form of its cytoplasmic domain fused to GFP, which partition exclusively in the nucleus, rescues cell migration.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: Addition of a soluble form of adam13 cytoplasmic domain fused to GFP, which partitions exclusively in the nucleus, rescues CNC migration.
source: In the absence of the cytoplasmic domain, adam13 cannot support CNC migration, but addition of a soluble form of its cytoplasmic domain fused to GFP, which partition exclusively in the nucleus, rescues cell migration.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: Addition of a single leucine in the cytoplasmic domain of adam13 that creates a nuclear export signal prevents adam13 ability to rescue CNC migration.
source: Similarly, addition of a single leucine in the cytoplasmic domain of adam13 that creates a nuclear export signal prevents adam13 ability to rescue CNC migration.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: The ability of adam13 to regulate cell migration and gene expression is shared by the cytoplasmic domains of adam13 orthologues from C-elegans to marsupial.
source: This ability to regulate cell migration and gene expression is shared by the cytoplasmic domains of adam13 orthologues from C-elegans to marsupial, as well as the cytoplasmic domains of adam19 from frog and mouse, demonstrating the evolutionary conservation of this role.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: The cytoplasmic domains of adam19 from frog and mouse can regulate cell migration and gene expression like adam13.
source: This ability to regulate cell migration and gene expression is shared by the cytoplasmic domains of adam13 orthologues from C-elegans to marsupial, as well as the cytoplasmic domains of adam19 from frog and mouse, demonstrating the evolutionary conservation of this role.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: The cytoplasmic domains of adam9 and adam10 cannot compensate for the loss of the adam13 cytoplasmic domain.
source: In contrast, the cytoplasmic domains of adam9 and adam10, which also translocate into the nucleus, cannot compensate for the loss of the adam13 cytoplasmic domain, revealing the specificity of this activity (Cousin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: The cytoplasmic domains of adam9 and adam10 translocate into the nucleus.
source: In contrast, the cytoplasmic domains of adam9 and adam10, which also translocate into the nucleus, cannot compensate for the loss of the adam13 cytoplasmic domain, revealing the specificity of this activity (Cousin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors.

claim: Adam13 co-transfected with pcdh8l in Hek293T cells produces an extracellular fragment of pcdh8l detected in conditioned media.
source: Western blot analysis of conditioned media from transfected cells shows the presence of the extracellular fragment of pcdh8l only when co-transfected with adam13 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Western blot data from transfected cells shows the fragment only with adam13.

claim: No pcdh8l fragment is observed when pcdh8l is co-transfected with the proteolytically inactive mutant adam13E/A.
source: No fragment was observed when pcdh8l was co-transfected with A13E/A suggesting that the proteolytic activity of adam13 is responsible for the cleavage of pcdh8l.
evidence: Western blot data shows no fragment with the inactive mutant.

claim: The proteolytic activity of adam13 is responsible for the cleavage of pcdh8l.
source: No fragment was observed when pcdh8l was co-transfected with A13E/A suggesting that the proteolytic activity of adam13 is responsible for the cleavage of pcdh8l.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the inactive mutant does not produce the fragment.

claim: The monoclonal antibody mAb 2F4 recognizes a protein of approximately 120 kDa expressed at stage 20.
source: This antibody recognizes a protein of the appropriate size (120 kDa), expressed at the appropriate stage (stage 20), localized to the CNC in whole mount immunostaining and to the plasma membrane of CNC cells in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the antibody.

claim: The monoclonal antibody mAb 2F4 localizes to the CNC in whole mount immunostaining.
source: This antibody recognizes a protein of the appropriate size (120 kDa), expressed at the appropriate stage (stage 20), localized to the CNC in whole mount immunostaining and to the plasma membrane of CNC cells in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the antibody.

claim: The monoclonal antibody mAb 2F4 localizes to the plasma membrane of CNC cells in vitro.
source: This antibody recognizes a protein of the appropriate size (120 kDa), expressed at the appropriate stage (stage 20), localized to the CNC in whole mount immunostaining and to the plasma membrane of CNC cells in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the antibody.

claim: The monoclonal antibody mAb 2F4 recognizes pcdh8l but not pcdh8 transfected in Hek293T cells.
source: We further confirmed that it recognizes pcdh8l but not pcdh8 transfected in Hek293T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is confirmed by western blot data in the figure supplement.

claim: At stage 20, the main protein recognized by mAb 2F4 is the full length pcdh8l at 120 kDa, but two minor shorter fragments can be seen at approximately 60 and 40 kDa.
source: At stage 20, the main protein recognized is the full length at 120 kDa, but two minor shorter fragments can be seen at ≈60 (1) and ≈40 kDa (2), respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in western blot data.

claim: The pcdh8l fragments at approximately 60 and 40 kDa increased in embryos injected with adam13 mRNA.
source: These fragments increased in embryos injected with the adam13 mRNA suggesting that adam13 can also cleave pcdh8l in vivo.
evidence: This is observed in western blot data from injected embryos.

claim: Adam13 can cleave pcdh8l in vivo.
source: These fragments increased in embryos injected with the adam13 mRNA suggesting that adam13 can also cleave pcdh8l in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in fragments upon adam13 overexpression.

claim: Injection of MO13-resistant adam13 mRNA significantly rescued CNC migration in embryos injected with MO13 (26% inhibition compared to 57% with MO13 alone).
source: Injection of a MO13-resistant adam13 mRNA significantly rescued CNC migration (26% inhibition).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiment data in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Injection of the pcdh8l extracellular fragment (EC1-4) mRNA rescued CNC migration significantly (47% inhibition) in embryos lacking adam13.
source: Injection of the pcdh8l extracellular fragment (EC1-4) mRNA rescued CNC migration significantly (47% inhibition), but less efficiently than the adam13 mRNA.
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiment data in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The pcdh8l extracellular fragment (EC1-4) rescued CNC migration less efficiently than adam13 mRNA.
source: Injection of the pcdh8l extracellular fragment (EC1-4) mRNA rescued CNC migration significantly (47% inhibition), but less efficiently than the adam13 mRNA.
evidence: This is shown by comparing the rescue percentages in the data.

claim: Full length pcdh8l mRNA rescued CNC migration in embryos lacking adam13 more efficiently (36% inhibition) than EC1-4.
source: Surprisingly, we found that loss of adam13 could be significantly rescued by the full length pcdh8l mRNA even more efficiently (36% inhibition) than with EC1-4, a phenomenon that was not observed for cadherin-11 (McCusker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiment data in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The rescue of adam13 loss by full length pcdh8l was not observed for cadherin-11.
source: Surprisingly, we found that loss of adam13 could be significantly rescued by the full length pcdh8l mRNA even more efficiently (36% inhibition) than with EC1-4, a phenomenon that was not observed for cadherin-11 (McCusker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous findings with cadherin-11.

claim: The loss of adam13 does not simply prevent the cleavage of pcdh8l but could also affect its expression, localization or function.
source: These results suggest that the loss of adam13 does not simply prevent the cleavage of pcdh8l but could also affect its expression, localization or function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that full length pcdh8l rescues better than the fragment alone.

claim: Adam13 knockdown reduces the expression of pcdh8l mRNA by 43% at stage 20.
source: In these conditions adam13 Knockdown (KD), which reduces the adam13 protein to undetectable levels (Figure 2C,A13 Pro-P and Mature-M) reduced the expression of pcdh8l mRNA by 43% (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 2A.

claim: 71% of embryos injected with MO13 (5 ng) into one blastomere showed reduced expression of pcdh8l on the injected side compared to the non-injected control side at stage 20.
source: We observed that at stage 20, 71% of the embryos showed a reduced expression of pcdh8l on the injected side when compared to the non-injected control side (Figure 2B, N = 31).
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization data in Figure 2B.

claim: The level of pcdh8l protein was significantly reduced in embryos injected with MO13 compared to non-injected embryos.
source: We also tested the protein level of pcdh8l by western blot, using mAb 2F4 (Figure 2C). When compared to non-injected embryos, the level of pcdh8l protein was significantly reduced.
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: CNC isolated from embryos injected with MO13 had a 36% reduction of pcdh8l mRNA compared to control CNC.
source: CNC isolated from embryos injected with MO13 had a 36% reduction of pcdh8l mRNA compared to control CNC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in the figure supplement.

claim: Western blot analysis with mAb 2F4 showed a reduction in pcdh8l protein in CNC from embryos injected with MO13.
source: Again, western blot analysis with 2F4 showed a similar trend for the pcdh8l protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in the figure supplement.

claim: Loss of adam13 results in a significant decrease of pcdh8l expression.
source: These results show that loss of adam13 results in a significant decrease of pcdh8l expression.
evidence: This is concluded from the mRNA and protein data showing reduced pcdh8l levels.

claim: Wild-type adam13 induces pcdh8l expression in naïve ectoderm (animal cap).
source: Analysis of mRNA levels show that wild-type adam13 induces pcdh8l expression whereas its catalytically inactive form (A13E/A), a mutant lacking the cytoplasmic domain (ΔCyto) and the isolated cytoplasmic domain (C13) all fail to induce expression of pcdh8l (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 3A.

claim: The catalytically inactive form of adam13 (A13E/A) fails to induce pcdh8l expression in naïve ectoderm.
source: Analysis of mRNA levels show that wild-type adam13 induces pcdh8l expression whereas its catalytically inactive form (A13E/A), a mutant lacking the cytoplasmic domain (ΔCyto) and the isolated cytoplasmic domain (C13) all fail to induce expression of pcdh8l (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 3A.

claim: Adam13 lacking the cytoplasmic domain (ΔCyto) fails to induce pcdh8l expression in naïve ectoderm.
source: Analysis of mRNA levels show that wild-type adam13 induces pcdh8l expression whereas its catalytically inactive form (A13E/A), a mutant lacking the cytoplasmic domain (ΔCyto) and the isolated cytoplasmic domain (C13) all fail to induce expression of pcdh8l (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 3A.

claim: The isolated cytoplasmic domain of adam13 (C13) fails to induce pcdh8l expression in naïve ectoderm.
source: Analysis of mRNA levels show that wild-type adam13 induces pcdh8l expression whereas its catalytically inactive form (A13E/A), a mutant lacking the cytoplasmic domain (ΔCyto) and the isolated cytoplasmic domain (C13) all fail to induce expression of pcdh8l (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 3A.

claim: Both the proteolytic activity and the cytoplasmic domain of adam13 are required for induction of pcdh8l expression.
source: These results show that adam13 can induce the expression of pcdh8l in naïve ectoderm and that both the proteolytic activity and the cytoplasmic domain are required for this function.
evidence: This is concluded from the data showing that mutants lacking either feature fail to induce pcdh8l.

claim: MO13 reduces tfap2α mRNA expression to 67% of control embryos at stage 20.
source: The real-time PCR data indicate that MO13 reduces tfap2α mRNA expression to 67% of control embryos (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 4A.

claim: Loss of adam13 reduces tfap2α mRNA expression on the injected side in 76% of embryos as shown by in situ hybridization.
source: In situ hybridization with a tfap2α probe shows that loss of adam13 reduces tfap2α mRNA expression on the injected side in 76% of the embryos (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4B.

claim: Adam13 knockdown results in a significant reduction of tfap2α promoter activity in dissected CNC explants.
source: Analysis of the luciferase activity in dissected CNC explants shows a significant reduction of the tfap2α promoter activity following adam13 KD (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by luciferase assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: The decrease in tfap2α promoter activity following adam13 KD is nearly identical to the observed reduction of the endogenous tfap2α mRNA.
source: This decrease is nearly identical to the observed reduction of the endogenous tfap2α mRNA (Figure 4A) suggesting that this reporter contains the key responsive elements regulated by adam13.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the luciferase and mRNA data.

claim: The tfap2α:luciferase reporter contains the key responsive elements regulated by adam13.
source: This decrease is nearly identical to the observed reduction of the endogenous tfap2α mRNA (Figure 4A) suggesting that this reporter contains the key responsive elements regulated by adam13.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between reporter and endogenous gene responses.

claim: Animal caps injected with adam13 RNA have a significant increase in tfap2α mRNA expression levels compared to non-injected control.
source: The results show that compared to non-injected control (NI), animal caps injected with adam13 RNA have a significant increase in tfap2α mRNA expression levels (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 5A.

claim: Both the cytoplasmic domain and the proteolytic activity of adam13 are required for the full expression of tfap2α in naïve ectoderm.
source: Similar to what was observed for pcdh8l, both the cytoplasmic domain and the proteolytic activity of adam13 are required for the full expression of tfap2α.
evidence: This is concluded from the data showing that mutants lacking either feature fail to fully induce tfap2α.

claim: Transfection of adam13 in Hek293T cells results in an almost 4-fold increase in tfap2α promoter activity.
source: As seen in Figure 5B, transfection of adam13 results in an almost 4-fold increase in tfap2α promoter activity.
evidence: This is shown by luciferase assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: Adam13 and adam19 can induce the tfap2α promoter in Hek293T cells while adam9 cannot.
source: As expected, only adam13 and adam19 could induce the expression of tfap2α while adam9 could not.
evidence: This is shown by luciferase assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of adam13 is critical for tfap2α induction in Hek293T cells.
source: In addition, the cytoplasmic domain of adam13 was critical for tfap2α induction.
evidence: This is shown by luciferase assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of adam13 alone is not able to induce tfap2α expression in Hek293T cells.
source: As seen for pcdh8l, the cytoplasmic domain alone was not able to induce tfap2α expression.
evidence: This is shown by luciferase assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: The proteolytically inactive adam13 (A13E/A) mutant can induce the tfap2α reporter in Hek293T cells, though less efficiently than wild type adam13.
source: In contrast to what was seen in the animal cap, the proteolytically inactive adam13 (A13E/A) mutant was able to induce the reporter even if less efficiently than the wild type adam13.
evidence: This is shown by luciferase assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: Injection of a tfap2α morpholino prevented the induction of both pcdh8l and tfap2α by adam13 in animal caps.
source: In contrast, injection of a tfap2α morpholino prevented the induction of both pcdh8l and tfap2αby adam13 (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Reduction of β-catenin does not prevent adam13 induction of pcdh8l or tfap2α in animal caps.
source: The results show that reduction of β-catenin does not prevent adam13 induction of pcdh8l or tfap2α(Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Adam13 up-regulation of tfap2α was inhibited by the morpholino to tfap2α, suggesting a positive feedback loop mechanism.
source: Interestingly adam13 up-regulation of tfap2α was also inhibited by the morpholino to tfap2α suggesting a positive feedback loop mechanism in which, tfap2α is involved in its own regulation by adam13 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tfap2α knockdown prevents adam13 induction of tfap2α.

claim: Arid3a-flag co-precipitated with adam13 when injected into embryos.
source: When injected into embryos, arid3a-flag co precipitated with adam13 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6A.

claim: The interaction between arid3a-flag and adam13 was lost when adam13 was knocked down.
source: This interaction was lost when adam13 was KD (MO13).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6A.

claim: FoxD3-myc co-precipitated with endogenous adam13 protein when injected into embryos.
source: Similarly when foxd3-myc RNA was injected in embryos either alone or with the adam13 MO, the foxd3 protein was co-precipitated with the endogenous adam13 protein and was absent when adam13 was KD (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B.

claim: FoxD3 co-precipitation with adam13 was absent when adam13 was knocked down.
source: Similarly when foxd3-myc RNA was injected in embryos either alone or with the adam13 MO, the foxd3 protein was co-precipitated with the endogenous adam13 protein and was absent when adam13 was KD (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B.

claim: Both arid3a and foxd3 can interact with adam13 in vivo.
source: These results show that both transcription factors can interact with adam13 in vivo.
evidence: This is concluded from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Arid3a knockdown efficiently prevented adam13 induction of both tfap2α and pcdh8l in animal caps.
source: The real-time PCR shows that while arid3a KD efficiently prevented adam13 induction of both tfap2α and pcdh8l, foxd3 KD had no effect.
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 7A-B.

claim: FoxD3 knockdown had no effect on adam13 induction of tfap2α and pcdh8l in animal caps.
source: The real-time PCR shows that while arid3a KD efficiently prevented adam13 induction of both tfap2α and pcdh8l, foxd3 KD had no effect.
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Loss or gain of adam13 function had no effect on arid3a and foxd3 expression in animal caps.
source: In these experiments, loss or gain of adam13 function had no effect on arid3a and foxd3 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by real-time PCR data in the figure supplement.

claim: Adam13 induces tfap2α and pcdh8l expression even when Smad2 is knocked down in animal caps.

claim: Arid3a expression is not regulated by adam13.

claim: The complex containing the cleaved arid3a and at least the adam13 cytoplasmic domain is free to translocate into the nucleus.
